s: A. Substantive due process and economic regulation.
In the Lochner era (1897–1937), the Court used liberty of contract to strike down maximum-hours laws (Lochner v. New York, 1905), minimum-wage laws (Adkins, 1923), and other economic regulation.
West Coast Hotel v. Parrish (1937) ended that era by upholding a minimum wage.
Nebbia v. New York (1934) had already sustained price regulation.
Economic and social-welfare legislation receives rational-basis review.
The law is valid if it is rationally related to a legitimate government interest, and courts will hypothesize a rationale the legislature might have had (Williamson v. Lee Optical, 1955).

United States v. Carolene Products (1938) footnote 4 explained when more searching review might be appropriate: specific Bill of Rights guarantees, distortions of the political process, and prejudice against "discrete and insular minorities."
Punitive damages are the one area of economic due process with teeth.
Grossly excessive awards violate due process (BMW v. Gore, 1996; State Farm v. Campbell, 2003, where single-digit ratios are generally the outer bound).
